## XI.1.2 Functors and natural transformations

Definition XI.1.2. A functor $F : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}'$ from the category $\mathcal{C}$ to the category $\mathcal{C}'$ consists of a map $F : \mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{C}) \to \mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{C}')$ and of a map $F : \mathrm{Hom}(\mathcal{C}) \to \mathrm{Hom}(\mathcal{C}')$ such that

(a) for any object $V \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{C})$, we have $F(\mathrm{id}_V) = \mathrm{id}_{F(V)}$,

(b) for any morphism $f \in \mathrm{Hom}(\mathcal{C})$, we have

$$
s (F (f)) = F (s (f)) \quad a n d \quad b (F (f)) = F (b (f)),
$$

(c) if $f,g$ are composable morphisms in the category $C$, we have

$$
s (F (f)) = F (s (f)) \quad a n d \quad b (F (f)) = F (b (f)),
$$

(c) if $f,g$ are composable morphisms in the category $C$, we have

$$
F (g \circ f) = F (g) \circ F (f).
$$

It is clear that if $F : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ and $G : \mathcal{C}^{\prime} \to \mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}$ are functors, then the composition $G F$ is a functor from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}.$ For any category $\mathcal{C}$ , there exists a functor $\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{C}}$ , called the identity functor of $\mathcal{C}$ , which is the identity on the objects and on the morphisms in $\mathcal{C}.$ The inclusion of a subcategory in a category is a functor.

Definition XI.1.3. Let F,G be functors from the category $\mathcal{C}$ to the category $\mathcal{C}^{\prime}.$ A natural transformation $\eta$ from F to G we write $\eta : F\to G$ is a family of morphisms $\eta(V):F(V)\rightarrow G(V)$ in $\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ indexed by the objects V of C such that, for any morphism f:V $\to W$ in $\mathcal{C}$ , the square

$$
\begin{array}{c c c} F (V) & \xrightarrow {\eta (V)} & G (V) \\ \downarrow F (f) & & \downarrow G (f) \\ F (W) & \xrightarrow {\eta (W)} & G (W) \end{array}
$$

commutes.

If, furthermore, $\eta(V)$ is an isomorphism of $\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ for any object V in $\mathcal{C}$ , we say that $\eta : F\to G$ is a natural isomorphism.

If $\eta : F\to G$ is a natural isomorphism, then the collection of all morphisms $\eta (V)^{-1}$ defines a natural isomorphism $\eta^{-1}$ from G to F. We next define the important concept of an equivalence of categories.

Definition XI.1.4. Let $F : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ be a functor. Then F is an equivalence of categories if there exist a functor G : $\mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{C}$ and natural isomorphisms

$$
\eta : \mathrm {i d} _ {\mathcal {D}} \rightarrow F G \quad a n d \quad \theta : G F \rightarrow \mathrm {i d} _ {\mathcal {C}}.
$$

We now give a useful criterion for a functor $F : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ to be an equivalence of categories. Let us first say that a functor $F : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ is essentially surjective if, for any object W of D, there exists an object V of C such that $F (V) \cong W$ in D. It is said to be faithful [resp. fully faithful] if, for any couple $(V,V^{\prime})$ of objects of C, the map

$$
F: \operatorname {H o m} _ {\mathcal {C}} \left(V, V ^ {\prime}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname {H o m} _ {\mathcal {D}} \left(F (V), F \left(V ^ {\prime}\right)\right)
$$

on morphisms is injective [resp. bijective].

Proposition XI.1.5. A functor $F : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ is an equivalence of categories if and only if F is essentially surjective and fully faithful.

Proposition XI.1.5. A functor $F : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ is an equivalence of categories if and only if F is essentially surjective and fully faithful.

Proof. (a) Suppose that $F$ is an equivalence. Then there exist a functor $G : \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{C}$ and natural isomorphisms $\eta : \mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{D}} \to F G$ and $\theta : G F \to \mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{C}}.$

The first isomorphism shows that $W \cong F (G (W))$ for any object $W$ of $\mathcal{D}.$ In other words, $F$ is essentially surjective. Now consider a morphism $f : V \to V^{\prime}$ in $\mathcal{C}.$ The square

$$
\begin{array}{c c c} G F (V) & \xrightarrow {\theta (V)} & V \\ \downarrow G F (f) & & \downarrow f \\ G F \left(V ^ {\prime}\right) & \xrightarrow {\theta \left(V ^ {\prime}\right)} & V ^ {\prime} \end{array}
$$

commutes. It results that if $F ( f )=F ( f^{\prime} )$ , hence $G F ( f )=G F ( f^{\prime} )$ , then we have $f=f^{\prime}$ . Therefore, the functor F is faithful. Using the natural isomorphism $\eta$ in a similar way, we prove that G is faithful too. Now consider a morphism $g: F ( V )\rightarrow F ( V^{\prime} )$ . Let us show that $g=F ( f )$ where $f=\theta( V^{\prime} )\circ G ( g)\circ \theta( V )^{-1}.$ Indeed,

$$
\theta \left(V ^ {\prime}\right) \circ G F (f) \circ \theta (V) ^ {- 1} = f = \theta \left(V ^ {\prime}\right) \circ G (g) \circ \theta (V) ^ {- 1}.
$$

Therefore $G F(f)=G(g)$ . As G is faithful, we get $g=F(f)$ . This proves that F is fully faithful.

(b) Let $F$ be an essentially surjective and fully faithful functor. For any object $W$ in $\mathcal{D}$ , we choose an object $G ( W )$ of $\mathcal{C}$ and an isomorphism $\eta ( W ) : W \to F G ( W )$ in $\mathcal{D}$ . If $g : W \to W^{\prime}$ is a morphism of $\mathcal{D}$ , we may consider

$$
\eta \left(W ^ {\prime}\right) \circ g \circ \eta (W) ^ {- 1}: F G (W) \rightarrow F G \left(W ^ {\prime}\right).
$$

Since F is fully faithful, there exists a unique morphism G(g) from G(W) to $G ( W^{\prime} )$ such that

$$
F G (g) = \eta \left(W ^ {\prime}\right) \circ g \circ \eta (W) ^ {- 1}: F G (W) \rightarrow F G \left(W ^ {\prime}\right).
$$

One checks easily that this defines a functor $G$ from $\mathcal{D}$ into $\mathcal{C}$ and that $\eta :\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{D}} \to F G$ is a natural isomorphism. In order to show that $F$ and $G$ are equivalences of categories, we have only to find a natural isomorphism $\theta : G F \to\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{C}}.$ We define $\theta(V): G F(V) \to V$ for any object $V\in\mathrm{O b}(\mathcal{C})$ as the unique morphism such that $F(\theta(V))=\eta(F(V))^{-1}.$ It is easily checked that this formula defines a natural isomorphism.

Corollary XI.1.6. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category and $\mathcal{C}'$ a subcategory of $\mathcal{C}$ such that any object of $\mathcal{C}$ is isomorphic to an object of $\mathcal{C}'$ and such that we have $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}'}(V,V^{\prime})=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(V,V^{\prime})$ for all $V,V^{\prime}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C}^{\prime})$ . Then the inclusion of $\mathcal{C}'$ into $\mathcal{C}$ is an equivalence of categories.

Example 3. (The groupoid $GL(k)$ ) Let $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(k)$ be the group of invertible matrices of order n with entries in a field k. Set $\mathrm{GL}_{0}(k)=\{1\}$ . By Example 1 we can associate to the family $(\mathrm{GL}_{n}(k))_{n\geq0}$ a groupoid denoted $GL(k)$ . By the previous corollary, the category $GL(k)$ is equivalent to the groupoid $(Vect_{f}(k))_{is}$ of all finite dimensional k-vector spaces whose morphisms are the linear isomorphisms.

Example 4. (The groupoid $\mathcal{S}$ ) Let $S_{n}$ be the symmetric group of all permutations of the finite set $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ . Set $S_{0}=\{1\}$ . Again by the construction of Example 1, we get a groupoid $\mathcal{S}$ . The category $\mathcal{S}$ is equivalent to the groupoid $(Set_{f})_{is}$ of finite sets whose morphisms are bijective.

## XI.1.3 Adjoint functors

We end these preliminaries on categories with the concept of adjoint functors. As we may observe from Proposition 1.8, as well from the examples of this section and the exercises of this chapter, the concept of adjoint functors is nothing but the categorical translation of the idea of a universal property.

Definition XI.1.7. Let F : $\mathcal{C} \rightarrow\mathcal{D}$ and G: $\mathcal{D} \rightarrow\mathcal{C}$ be functors. Then F is right adjoint to G or G is left adjoint to F if there exist natural transformations $\eta :\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{D}} \rightarrow F G$ and $\theta : G F \rightarrow\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{C}}$ such that the composite

$$
F (V) \xrightarrow {\eta (F (V))} (F G F) (V) \xrightarrow {F (\theta (V))} F (V)
$$

and

$$
F (V) \xrightarrow {\eta (F (V))} (F G F) (V) \xrightarrow {F (\theta (V))} F (V)
$$

and

$$
G (W) \xrightarrow {G (\eta (W))} (G F G) (W) \xrightarrow {\theta (G (W))} G (W)
$$

are identity morphisms for all objects V of C and W in D.

The following characterizes adjoint functors in terms of natural bijections.

Proposition XI.1.8. Let F : $\mathcal{C} \rightarrow\mathcal{D}$ and G: $\mathcal{D} \rightarrow\mathcal{C}$ be functors. Then F is right adjoint to G if and only if for all objects V in $\mathcal{C}$ and all objects W in $\mathcal{D}$ there exists a natural bijection

$$
\Phi (V, W): \operatorname {H o m} _ {\mathcal {C}} (G (W), V) \rightarrow \operatorname {H o m} _ {\mathcal {D}} (W, F (V)),
$$

i. e., such that, for all morphisms f in $\mathcal{C}$ and all morphisms g in $\mathcal{D}$ , the diagram

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname {H o m} _ {\mathcal {C}} \left(G \left(W ^ {\prime}\right), V\right) \xrightarrow {\Phi \left(V, W ^ {\prime}\right)} \operatorname {H o m} _ {\mathcal {D}} \left(W ^ {\prime}, F (V)\right) \\ \downarrow_ {\operatorname {H o m} (G (g), V)} \quad \downarrow_ {\operatorname {H o m} (g, F (V))} \\ \operatorname {H o m} _ {\mathcal {C}} \left(G (W), V\right) \xrightarrow {\Phi \left(V, W\right)} \operatorname {H o m} _ {\mathcal {D}} \left(W, F (V)\right) \\ \downarrow_ {\operatorname {H o m} (G (W), f)} \quad \downarrow_ {\operatorname {H o m} (W, F (f))} \\ \operatorname {H o m} _ {\mathcal {C}} \left(G (W), V ^ {\prime}\right) \xrightarrow {\Phi \left(V ^ {\prime}, W\right)} \operatorname {H o m} _ {\mathcal {D}} \left(W, F \left(V ^ {\prime}\right)\right) \\ \end{array}
$$

commutes where $V = s(f), V^{\prime} = b(f), W = s(g)$ and $W^{\prime} = b(g).$

Proof. The vertical maps of the above diagram are the obvious maps obtained by composition with f, F(f), g, and G(g). We sketch the proof of this proposition. For details, see [Mac71], Chapter IV.

(a) Let $F$ be a right adjoint to $G$. Set $\Phi(V, W)(f) = F(f)\circ \eta(W)$ for any morphism $f: G(W)\rightarrow V$, and $\Psi(V, W)(g) = \theta(V)\circ G(g)$ for any morphism $g: W\rightarrow F(V)$. Using the definition of adjoint functors, one checks that the map $\Phi(V, W)$ is bijective with inverse $\Psi(V, W)$.

(b) Suppose given the bijections $\Phi (V, W).$ We have to construct natural transformations $\eta :\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{D}}\rightarrow FG$ and $\theta:GF\rightarrow\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{C}}.$ They are defined by

$$
\eta (W) = \Phi (G (W), W) (\mathrm {i d} _ {G (W)}) \quad \text {a n d} \quad \theta (V) = \Phi^ {- 1} (V, F (V)) (\mathrm {i d} _ {F (V)}).
$$

The reader will easily check that $\eta$ and $\theta$ are natural transformations.

An equivalence of categories is always left and right adjoint to another equivalence. We give two examples of adjoint functors already encountered in this book.

$$

Definition XI.2.1. A tensor category $(\mathcal{C},\otimes ,I,a,l,r)$ is a category $\mathcal{C}$ which is equipped with a tensor product $\otimes :\mathcal{C}\times \mathcal{C}\rightarrow \mathcal{C}$ , with an object I, called the unit of the tensor category, with an associativity constraint a, a left unit constraint l and a right unit constraint r with respect to I such that the Pentagon Axiom (2.6) and the Triangle Axiom (2.9) are satisfied.

The tensor category is said to be strict if the associativity and unit constraints a,l,r are all identities of the category.

Examples of tensor categories will be given in Section 3.

## XI.3 Examples of Tensor Categories

In this book we shall be concerned with two main types of tensor categories. The first type is built on vector spaces and their tensor products as introduced in Chapter II. The second one uses the 1-dimensional objects of Chapter X such as links, tangles and braids. We shall connect both types in Chapter XII.

## XI.3.1 Tensor categories of vector spaces

The most fundamental example of a tensor category is given by the category $\mathcal{C}=Vect(k)$ of vector spaces over a field k. The latter is equipped with a tensor structure for which $\otimes$ is the tensor product (defined in II.1) of the vector spaces over k, the unit object I is the ground field k itself, and the associativity and unit constraints are the natural isomorphisms

$$
